title-group.article-title: Sustainable Utilization of Agricultural By-Products: in vivo investigation of the antidiarrheal potential of Litchi chinensis seed extract

sec.title: Objectives
sec.p: Diarrheal diseases remain a significant global health concern, with rising resistance to traditional pharmaceutical treatments. Litchi chinensis, a tropical fruit, is known for its medicinal properties, but its seed, which is often discarded as waste, has not been extensively studied for its potential health benefits. This study investigates the antidiarrheal effects of L. chinensis seed extract (LCSE).

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Ethanolic extract was prepared from dried, powdered L. chinensis seeds. Acute oral toxicity was conducted by administering a single 2,000 mg/kg dose to female Swiss albino mice. Mice were divided into five groups (control, positive control with Loperamide, and test groups receiving 100, 200, and 400 mg/kg of LCSE) for the antidiarrheal assay. Diarrhea was induced with castor oil, and parameters such as onset of diarrhea, fecal output, gastrointestinal motility, and enteropooling were measured. The statistical analysis was conducted in GraphPad Prism version 10.1.2 using one-way ANOVA followed by a Dunnett multiple comparison test.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: L. chinensis seed extract (LCSE) significantly (p < 0.001) delayed the onset of diarrhea, reduced the frequency of defecation, and decreased fecal weight in the castor oil-induced diarrhea model at all doses (100, 200, and 400 mg/kg). Additionally, LCSE significantly (p < 0.001) reduced total and wet fecal output, inhibited gastrointestinal motility (p < 0.001) in the charcoal meal test, and notably (p < 0.001) decreased the volume and weight of intestinal contents in the enteropooling assay. The in vivo antidiarrheal index (ADI) showed a dose-dependent increase, with the highest ADI recorded at 400 mg/kg (189.42%), slightly surpassing the standard drug, loperamide (160.14%).

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The finding supports the antidiarrheal potential of LCSE holds potent antidiarrheal properties, positioning it as a promising, sustainable alternative to modern medications.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Diarrhea is a gastrointestinal (GI) disorder characterized by the frequent passage of loose or watery stools, typically occurring three or more times within 24 h, often accompanied by increased stool volume, fluidity, and abdominal discomfort [1]. It is primarily caused by bacterial (e.g., Escherichia coli [E. coli], Salmonella spp., Shigella spp., and Campylobacter spp.), viral (e.g., rotavirus, norovirus, and sapovirus), and parasitic pathogens (e.g., Cryptosporidium, Giardia, and Entamoeba spp.) [2]. Early antibiotic exposure has been associated with a higher incidence of diarrhea during early childhood [3]. Diarrheal disease remains the third leading cause of death globally, accounting for approximately 2 million deaths or 4% of global mortality [4]. It causes an estimated 1.3 million child deaths annually, and by 2030, approximately 4.4 million children might die from infectious diseases, including diarrhea [5]. South Africa and Southeast Asia contribute to 80% of diarrheal deaths in children aged under 5 years in developing countries, with Bangladesh ranking seventh in diarrhea-related mortality [6]. In Bangladesh, an estimated 28 million cases occur annually among children aged under 5 years [7], with an 8.78% increase in 2019 [5]. Diarrhea is a major contributor to malnutrition in children aged under 5 years in developing countries [4]. Despite global efforts to reduce its prevalence, diarrheal disease remains widespread. Treatment options, such as antimotility drugs, adsorbents, and anticholinergics, help reduce adult symptom frequency [8]. However, these therapies present several limitations, including adverse effects such as abdominal discomfort, xerostomia, fever, nausea, dependency, cephalalgia, vertigo, epigastric distress, rashes, eosinophilia, allergic reactions, and dermal eruptions [9].

However, due to potential adverse effects and the risk of worsening illness in certain cases, these medications are not recommended for use in children or infants [8]. The rise of antibiotic-resistant bacterial strains associated with diarrhea, including multidrug-resistant E. coli, Vibrio cholerae, Salmonella spp., and Shigella spp. in Bangladesh, highlights the urgent need for alternative therapeutic strategies [10]. Therefore, the World Health Organization (WHO) advocates for research into the prevention and treatment of GI diseases using conventional remedies. As part of its Diarrhea Control Program, the WHO has integrated traditional medicine to mitigate the burden of diarrhea [11]. According to the WHO, approximately 90% of the global population relies primarily on conventional therapies, with plant-based treatments comprising a substantial portion [12]. Herbal medicines have garnered increasing attention for their therapeutic efficacy, purity, and affordability [13]. Historically, various herbs have been used to manage infectious diseases such as bronchitis, cutaneous abscesses, diarrhea, parasitic infections, and urinary tract infections [11]. Several studies report that extracts from medicinal plants exhibit antidiarrheal effects through mechanisms including antispasmodic activity, delayed GI transit, reduced gut motility, enhanced water absorption, and/or reduced electrolyte secretion [9].

In this context, the litchi (Litchi chinensis Sonn., Sapindaceae [L. chinensis]) is a tropical fruit tree native to southern China, cultivated worldwide in semi-tropical regions for its edible, white, translucent aril. The aril is consumed fresh and used in products such as juice, vinegar, jam, jelly, ice cream, and wine [14]. Litchi seeds are dark brown or chocolate-colored, oblong to concave in shape, and measure approximately 1-3.3 cm in length and 0.6-1.2 cm in width [15]. Litchi has been employed in traditional Chinese medicine for treating stomach ulcers, diabetes, cough, diarrhea, dyspepsia, and intestinal parasitic infections [16]. Ethnopharmacological evidence suggests that the seeds are used to eliminate pathogenic colds, alleviate stagnant humor, and act as an analgesic in conditions such as orchitis, neuralgia, testicular edema, hernia, and abdominal pain. Additionally, the seeds possess antioxidant [15], antidiabetic [17], antibacterial, and anthelmintic [14] properties. Despite these benefits, litchi seeds are typically discarded and remain underutilized. Global litchi production is estimated at approximately 2.7 million tons annually, generating around 0.54 million tons of seeds [18]. Processing yields 30-40% by-products, of which approximately 20% are seeds, posing significant environmental and economic challenges for the industry [15]. The absence of pharmacological screening for the traditional use of L. chinensis seeds (LCS) in treating diarrhea, alongside existing ethnomedical evidence, supports the rationale for this study. This study aimed to evaluate the antidiarrheal efficacy of crude ethanolic LCS extract (LCSE) in experimental animal models.

sec.title: 1. Drug and chemicals
sec.p: All chemicals and reagents used in the physiochemical analysis, quantitative assessment of secondary metabolites, qualitative inorganic nutrient test, and antidiarrheal assays were of analytical grade. Castor oil (WELL’s Heath Care, Spain), loperamide (Square Pharmaceuticals Ltd., Bangladesh), activated charcoal (Labchem Industries, India), and ethanol (Sigma-Aldrich, USA) were procured from licensed suppliers.

sec.title: 2. Collection and preparation of LCS crude powder
sec.p: Fruits of L. chinensis were obtained from a local market in Ishwardi, Pabna District, Bangladesh, in June 2024. The species was identified and authenticated by the Head of the Department of Botany, Chuadanga Government College, Chuadanga, and taxonomically verified using a voucher specimen (voucher number: CDGC/DOB/2023/09). A corresponding specimen was also deposited at the Bangladesh National Herbarium under accession number 41495. The pericarp and arils were carefully removed, and the seeds were separated, washed with distilled water to eliminate surface contaminants, and cut into small pieces using a sterile blade. The seed pieces were initially air-dried in a well-ventilated, shaded environment, followed by incubation at 40℃ to remove residual moisture. The dried seeds were then ground into a fine powder using an automated grinder and stored in hermetically sealed containers [14].

sec.title: 3. LCSE preparation
sec.p: Forty grams of LCS powder was combined with 400 mL of high-purity ethanol in a dark glass bottle wrapped in aluminum foil. The mixture was agitated in a shaking incubator at 37℃ for 96 h. After extraction, the solution was filtered using Whatman filter paper Grade 1, and the filtrate was dried by incubation at 50-55℃. The resulting extract was stored in sterile bottles at 4℃ until further use [14].

sec.title: 4. Extraction yield of LCS
sec.p: Ten grams of LCS powder was accurately weighed and packed in a dark, corked glass bottle containing 100 mL of ethanol. The mixture was stirred in a shaking incubator at 37℃ for 96 h. It was then filtered using Whatman filter paper Grade 1, and the filtrate was concentrated in an incubator at 50-55℃. The extraction yield was subsequently calculated as a percentage [17].

sec.title: 5. Study animals
sec.p: Swiss albino mice of both sexes (weight: 20-30 g; age: 6-8 weeks) were procured from Jahangirnagar University, Dhaka, Bangladesh. The mice were housed in standard cages, under a 12-h light/dark cycle at a controlled temperature of 22 ± 2℃, with ad libitum access to pellet food and water. They were acclimatized to laboratory conditions for 7 days before the experimental procedure. All procedures involving animals complied with internationally accepted guidelines for the care and use of experimental animals [19] and were approved by the Ethical Review Committee of the Faculty of Biological Sciences Islamic University, Kushtia, Bangladesh (reference number: FBS/ERC/IU/2024/05, date: 03.02.2024).

sec.title: 6. Acute oral toxicity test
sec.p: The acute oral toxicity test was conducted following the guidelines of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development [20]. Female Swiss albino mice (weight: 20-30 g; age: 6-8 weeks) were used for the assessment. Initially, a single fasted female mouse received an oral loading dose of 2,000 mg/kg of ethanolic LCSE via gavage. The mouse was closely monitored for signs of toxicity, including behavioral changes, weakness, aggression, anorexia, diarrhea, salivation, convulsions, injuries, and ocular or auricular discharges, with particular focus during the initial 4 h and again at 24 h post-administration. As no mortality occurred within 24 h, four additional female mice were administered the same dose. All animals were then observed every 30 min for the first 4 h and subsequently once daily for 14 consecutive days to monitor general clinical signs of toxicity.

sec.title: 1) Grouping and dosing of animals
sec.p: Thirty Swiss albino mice, equally distributed by sex, were used in each antidiarrheal model and randomly allocated into five groups (n = 6 per group). The treatment groups were as follows:
Group I: The negative control group received distilled water (10 mL/kg)
Group II: The positive control group, received loperamide (3 mg/kg)
Groups III: The test group, received LCSE (100 mg/kg)
Groups IV: The test group, received LCSE (200 mg/kg)
Groups V: The test group, received LCSE (400 mg/kg)

sec.title: 2) Castor oil-induced diarrhea
sec.p: Diarrhea was induced in mice using castor oil according to a previously established protocol with minor modification [21]. Before treatment, all rats were fasted for 18 h with ad libitum access to water. Mice were randomly assigned to treatment groups as described in Section 2.7.1. One hour after administering the test substances, each mouse received 0.5 mL of castor oil orally. Mice were individually placed in separate transparent plastic cages lined with non-wetting white paper, which was replaced hour for 4 h. During the observation period, the time of onset of diarrhea (defined as the interval in minutes between castor oil administration and the first diarrheal episode), frequency and weight of wet stools, and total fecal output, were recorded. The antidiarrheal effects were assessed using the following formulas:

sec.title: 3) Castor oil-induced GI motility
sec.p: A GI motility test was performed in accordance with previously described methods [22]. The mice were fasted for 18 h before the experiment, with ad libitum access to water, and randomly allocated into five treatment groups. One hour after administering the respective treatments, each mouse received 0.5 mL of castor oil orally to induce GI motility. After an additional 60 min, 1 mL of a 5% activated charcoal suspension in distilled water was administered orally to each mouse. Thirty min following the charcoal administration, the mice were euthanized via cervical dislocation. The abdominal cavity was opened, and the small intestine was excised, extending from the pylorus to the caecum. The intestine was carefully laid out on a white sheet of paper, and the total length of the small intestine and the distance traveled by the charcoal marker were measured using a standardized ruler. The peristaltic index (PI) and percentage inhibition of GI motility were calculated using the following formulas:

sec.title: 4) Castor oil-induced enteropooling
sec.p: The enteropooling assay was performed following a standard protocol with slight modifications [21]. Before the experiment, the mice were fasted for 18 h with free access to water. They were then randomly allocated into the predefined groups and treated according to the specified dosages. One hour after the oral administration of castor oil (0.5 mL), the mice were euthanized via cervical dislocation. The abdominal cavity of each mouse was opened, and the small intestine, extending from the pylorus to the cecum, was carefully ligated, dissected, and excised. Intestinal contents were expelled by gently milking the intestine into a graduated tube to allow for volumetric analysis. The percentage reduction in intestinal fluid volume and weight was calculated using the following formulas:

sec.title: 8. Statistical analysis
sec.p: All statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism (version 10.1.2; GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA). The antidiarrheal effects of the treatments were evaluated through one-way analysis of variance, followed by Dunnett’s multiple comparison test. Data are presented as mean ± standard error of the mean for each group (n = 6), differences were considered statistically significant at p < 0.05.

sec.title: 1. Extraction efficacy of LCS
sec.p: The extraction yield of 11.09 ± 0.26% was obtained, as presented in Table 1.

sec.title: 2. Acute oral toxicity test
sec.p: No signs of toxicity or mortality were observed during the 2-week observational period following a single oral dose of 2,000 mg/kg LCSE. The absence of adverse effects at a dose five times higher than the maximum effective dose suggests a wide safety margin for LCSE, with a median lethal dose exceeding 2,000 mg/kg in mice.

sec.title: 3. Body weight and fecal consistency
sec.p: Table 2 presents the effects of LCS extracts (LCSE) on fecal consistency and body weight in mice with castor oil-induced diarrhea. On Day 0, all groups exhibited loose, watery stools. By Day 3, the control group continued to show loose, watery stools and experienced a 25.79% reduction in body weight. In contrast, LCSE-treated groups demonstrated dose-dependent improvements in fecal consistency, transitioning from loose to normal stools, alongside attenuated body weight loss. Notably, the 400 mg/kg LCSE group showed normalization of fecal output only a 7.45% reduction in body weight, compared to a 9.90% decrease observed with the standard antidiarrheal drug loperamide. These findings suggest that LCSE ameliorates diarrhea symptoms in a dose-dependent manner, as evidenced by improved fecal consistency and mitigated body weight loss.

sec.title: 4. Castor oil-induced diarrhea
sec.p: The antidiarrheal efficacy of LCSE against castor oil-induced diarrhea in mice is summarized in Table 3. LCSE administration resulted in a dose-dependent delay in the onset of diarrhea. At doses of 100, 200, and 400 mg/kg, the onset was significantly prolonged to 48.46 ± 2.92, 83.50 ± 3.86, and 189.65 ± 4.77 min, respectively (p < 0.0001 for all), compared to 13.78 ± 0.40 min in the control group. The total number of fecal outputs was also markedly reduced in a dose-dependent manner: 7.12 ± 0.51 (p < 0.001) at 100 mg/kg, 5.22 ± 0.52 (p < 0.0001) at 200 mg/kg, and 2.25 ± 0.30 (p < 0.0001) at 400 mg/kg, compared to 9.55 ± 0.71 in the control group. The number of wet feces showed a significant reduction at all tested doses, 3.97 ± 0.69 at 100 mg/kg (p < 0.01), 2.43 ± 0.35 at 200 mg/kg (p < 0.0001), and 1.30 ± 0.19 at 400 mg/kg (p < 0.001), versus 6.74 ± 0.47 in the control group. Correspondingly, the total weight of wet feces and the total fecal output were significantly decreased, particularly at 400 mg/kg, with values of 0.09 ± 0.01 g and 0.18 ± 0.03 g (p < 0.0001 for both), compared to 0.60 ± 0.16 g and 0.88 ± 0.12 g in the control group. Although the standard drug loperamide (3 mg/kg) also reduced fecal parameters, the highest LCSE dose demonstrated superior efficacy. Fig. 1 further illustrates the dose-dependent effects of LCSE, with reductions in wet fecal output of 41.06%, 63.96%, and 80.67% at 100, 200, and 400 mg/kg, respectively, versus 78.67% with loperamide. Similarly, reductions in total fecal output were 54.06% at 100 mg/kg, 43.86% at 200 mg/kg, and 19.85% at 400 mg/kg, indicating a significant therapeutic potential of LCSE, particularly at the highest tested doses.

sec.title: 5. Intestinal transit of charcoal meal
sec.p: LCSE produced a dose-dependent reduction in GI transit, indicated by a progressive decline in PI and corresponding percentage inhibition, as illustrated in Fig. 2. The control group exhibited a PI of 76.32 ± 5.24, reflecting normal GI motility. In contrast, treatment with LCSE at 100, 200, and 400 mg/kg significantly reduced the PI to 51.04 ± 8.38 (33.12% inhibition, p < 0.05), 37.07 ± 7.20 (51.42% inhibition, p < 0.01), and 24.67 ± 3.86 (67.68% inhibition, p < 0.0001), respectively. The standard drug, loperamide (3 mg/kg) significantly reduced the PI to 28.88 ± 6.10 (62.16% inhibition, p < 0.0001). Notably, the inhibitory effect of LCSE at 400 mg/kg suppressed that of loperamide, suggesting a comparable or superior efficacy at higher doses.

sec.title: 6. Castor oil-induced enteropooling
sec.p: In this study, LCSE and the standard drug loperamide (3 mg/kg), significantly reduced intraluminal fluid accumulation, as indicated by decreases in the volume and weight of intestinal contents. At a dose of 200 mg/kg (p < 0.05) and 400 mg/kg (p < 0.001), LCSE significantly reduced intestinal fluid accumulation compared to the control group (Table 4). The reductions in intestinal fluid volume and weight at 200 mg/kg were 44.92% and 40.22%, respectively, while at 400 mg/kg, the reductions increased to 60.35% and 54.10%. Loperamide (3 mg/kg) also produced significant reductions of 52.54% in volume and 49.84% in weight. Notably, LCSE at 400 mg/kg exhibited slightly higher inhibition of intestinal fluid accumulation than loperamide.

sec.title: 7. In vivo ADI
sec.p: The ADI of LCSE exhibited a dose-dependent increase, with the highest ADI observed at the maximum dose of 400 mg/kg (189.42%). This value slightly surpassed that of the standard drug loperamide, which demonstrated an ADI of 160.14%, as presented in Table 5.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: In Bangladesh, medicinal plants have been traditionally employed for centuries to treat a wide range of health conditions, including malaria, diarrhea, dysentery, fungal infections, and respiratory infections. Among these, L. chinensis has a longstanding history of use in managing GI conditions such as ulcers, gastritis, infections, and diarrhea [14]. Recent investigations into the antidiarrheal efficacy of plant-derived extracts in animal models highlight the growing need for scientific validation of traditional medicinal practices [23]. In this context, the present study was designed to evaluate the safety and antidiarrheal efficacy of LCS, thereby substantiating its traditional use through experimental evidence.

In this study, the extraction yield of LCS is presented in Table 1. The alcohol-soluble extraction yield (11.09 ± 0.26%) indicates that a significant proportion of phytochemicals, particularly phenolic compounds or flavonoids, are soluble in polar organic solvents such as ethanol. Ethanol not only serves as an effective extraction medium but also possesses antimicrobial properties that help prevent contamination. These findings contribute to a foundational understanding of LCSE and can aid in establishing standardized benchmarks for evaluating its efficacy in future pharmaceutical applications. The antidiarrheal potential of LCS was evaluated using the castor oil-induced diarrhea model, a widely accepted experimental system for screening antidiarrheal agents. Castor oil induces diarrhea by releasing ricinoleic acid, a metabolite that [8] irritates the GI mucosa and stimulates prostaglandin production [24]. These prostaglandins enhance GI motility and promote electrolyte secretion, resulting in reduced electrolyte absorption in the intestine and colon, thereby resulting in diarrhea [25]. Additionally, castor oil suppresses the activity of intestinal sodium/potassium-adenosine triphosphatase, further reducing fluid absorption and contributing to diarrhea [26]. Loperamide, a synthetic opioid and standard reference drug in antidiarrheal studies, was employed as a positive control. It exerts its effects by activating μ-opioid receptors in the myenteric plexus of the large intestine [27]. μ-opioid receptors are primarily located on the presynaptic terminals of parasympathetic cholinergic nerve fibers in the smooth muscle layers of the intestine [28]. Activation of these receptors by loperamide inhibits the release of acetylcholine, resulting in decreased smooth muscle tone within the intestinal wall [27, 29]. This mechanism promotes segmentation contractions in the colon while inhibiting peristalsis, thereby prolonging intestinal transit time. Additionally, by reducing acetylcholine-mediated secretion, loperamide effectively decreases intestinal fluid output [30]. Collectively, these actions lead to reduced fecal volume, minimized fluid and electrolyte loss, and increased stool viscosity and bulk. Similarly, LCSE exhibited a dose-dependent improvement in fecal consistency (Table 2), with higher doses significantly enhancing the consistency of feces and mitigating body weight loss. At the highest dose (400 mg/kg), fecal consistency improved from loose, watery stools to a normal form, mirroring the effects of loperamide. This suggests that LCSE possesses substantial antidiarrheal activity, potentially offering a viable alternative to conventional treatments. In the castor oil-induced diarrhea model (Table 3, Fig. 1), LCSE demonstrated significant efficacy across multiple parameters. These included delayed onset of diarrhea, reductions in the total number and weight of feces, and a marked decrease in the number of wet feces. The findings revealed that administration of LCSE at a dose of 400 mg/kg led to a significant reduction in several key diarrheal parameters when compared to the control group. These included a delayed onset of diarrhea (p < 0.0001), reduced total fecal count (p < 0.0001), lower total fecal weight (p < 0.01), and fewer wet fecal episodes (p < 0.001). Notably, the percentage inhibition of wet feces at this dose reached 80.67%, marginally exceeding the inhibition observed with the standard drug loperamide (78.67%). These findings are consistent with previous reports demonstrating that higher doses of LCSE, specifically 400 mg/kg, are most effective in managing diarrhea [28, 31]. Prior studies have attributed the pharmacological effects of L. chinensis to its ability to inhibit prostaglandin biosynthesis, thereby exerting analgesic and anti-inflammatory activities analogous to non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs [32]. Given that most antidiarrheal drugs function by suppressing intestinal fluid secretion or attenuating GI motility [33], the observed effects of LCSE are consistent with known mechanisms of action. Furthermore, in the castor oil-induced enteropooling assay (Table 3), LCSE significantly (p < 0.05) reduced intraluminal fluid accumulation compared to the negative control group. At the highest tested dose (400 mg/kg), LCSE produced a marginally greater inhibitory effect on enteropooling than Loperamide. This observation supports earlier findings involving Valeriana officinalis root extracts, which similarly demonstrated dose-dependent reductions in intestinal fluid secretion. The anti-enteropooling activity of LCSE may be attributed to its rich phytochemical composition, particularly the presence of flavonoids, tannins, terpenoids, and alkaloids, as previously identified in its bioactive profile [14]. Flavonoids can inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, thereby reducing castor oil-induced intestinal secretion and facilitating enhanced electrolyte uptake [34]. Tannins contribute to antidiarrheal effects by decreasing intestinal fluid secretion, primarily by inhibiting cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator and calcium-activated chloride channels. Additionally, they form protein-tannin complexes in the intestinal lining [35]. Terpenoids exert antidiarrheal effects by attenuating prostaglandin-mediated release and modulating peristalsis [35, 36]. Similarly, alkaloids have been reported to slow intestinal propulsion by altering electrolyte and water absorption [25]. The pronounced antidiarrheal activity observed in this study is likely attributed to the interactions among the phytochemicals in LCSE. In the small intestinal transit test (Fig. 2), LCSE exhibited a dose-dependent inhibition of gastrointestinal motility, with the highest effect observed at 400 mg/kg. The charcoal meal test was employed for its relevance in assessing antidiarrheal agents that act via suppression of peristalsis—a common therapeutic mechanism among conventional antidiarrheal drugs [37]. LCSE significantly inhibited the intestinal transit of the charcoal meal (Table 4), thereby prolonging the contact time for nutrient and water absorption in the GI tract [38]. This antimotility effect aligns with previous findings on the efficacy of Lantana camara leaf extracts in reducing intestinal secretion at higher doses [31]. Furthermore, the antidiarrheal efficacy of LCSE (Table 5) is substantiated by its in vivo ADI value, which quantifies the effectiveness of LCSE in diarrheal management [35]. Typically, higher ADI values correlate with greater effectiveness in treating diarrhea [21]. In the current study, the ADI increased in a dose-dependent manner, with the maximum efficacy observed at the highest dose of LCSE (400 mg/kg). These findings are consistent with previous studies that highlighted enhanced antidiarrheal activity at elevated extract concentrations [28], thereby reinforcing the pharmacological potential of LCSE. Future studies should prioritize the isolation and quantification of its bioactive compounds using advanced techniques such as high-performance liquid chromatography and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry to further elucidate the mechanisms underlying the antidiarrheal activity of LCSE. Additionally, molecular mechanism-based studies, including gene expression analysis, enzyme inhibition assays, antimotility evaluations, and receptor interaction studies, will be essential for a more comprehensive pharmacodynamic understanding. Long-term toxicity studies are necessary to ensure the safety of LCSE for clinical use. Moreover, evaluating its therapeutic efficacy in treating other GI disorders, such as irritable bowel syndrome and inflammatory bowel disease, could expand its therapeutic potential.

sec.title: CONCLUSION
sec.p: The findings of this study demonstrate that LCSE exhibits significant antidiarrheal properties. LCSE demonstrated significant efficacy across multiple experimental models, including castor oil-induced diarrhea, GI motility, and enteropooling assays. The extract produced a dose-dependent reduction in fecal output, delayed diarrhea onset, and inhibited GI motility. Notably, the highest tested dose (400 mg/kg) exhibited comparable antidiarrheal activity to loperamide. Additionally, LCSE exhibited no signs of acute toxicity, indicating its safety at therapeutic doses. Collectively, these findings highlight the potential of LCSE as a safe, natural, and environmentally sustainable alternative to conventional antidiarrheal agents, warranting further research to explore its broader medicinal applicability.
